claims.text: The fossil fuels are coal, oil and natural gas, formed from ancient plant and animal remains over millions of years. They are non-renewable because they are being used up far faster than new ones form, and together they still supplied about 80 per cent of world energy in the early 2020s (rounded figure).

claims.text: Energy use differs with a country's level of development. High-income countries use several times more energy per person, because industry, motor transport and heated or cooled homes all draw power. Many low-income countries use little energy per person and rely mainly on fuelwood and other biomass gathered locally for cooking and heating, which takes hours to collect and can strip woodland around towns.

claims.text: The fossil fuels are coal, oil and natural gas alone. Petrol is not itself a fossil fuel - it is refined from oil, so it is a product of one - and hydro-electric power is renewable, because water is not used up. The test: is it a raw fuel formed from ancient remains?

claims.text: Nuclear power generates roughly a tenth of the world's electricity (early 2020s, rounded), mostly in higher-income countries, and a small volume of uranium yields a very large output, so fuel deliveries are light for the energy produced.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Nuclear power's benefits: one station generates a large, steady output for decades, so a few stations can supply a whole grid; generation releases no carbon dioxide, so it does not add to the enhanced greenhouse effect the way burning coal or gas does; and the fuel volumes are small, so deliveries are light.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Nuclear power's disadvantages: its radioactive waste must be stored safely for very long periods, which no country finds easy; stations are very expensive to build and later to take apart; and an accident can spread contamination over a wide area, as at Chernobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011.

claims.text: Renewable sources are cheaper to run once built, because they need no fuel, but the installations are often expensive to build and their output is intermittent: the wind drops and the sun sets, so wind and solar need back-up stations or storage, which adds to the building bill.

claims.text: Carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels enhances the greenhouse effect, trapping more heat and warming the climate. It does not thin the ozone layer - that is a separate problem caused mainly by CFC gases - so the two are not the same thing.

claims.text: Namibia's largest domestic power station is the hydro plant at Ruacana on the Kunene River in the far north-west, capacity about 340 megawatts (2010s figure). Roughly half the country's electricity was imported in the 2010s (rounded), and solar farms have been added since the mid-2010s, in a country with more than 3 000 hours of sunshine a year.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Namibia's supply is shaped by its physical and economic geography: the population is small and thinly spread, so the domestic market is too small to repay many large stations; most rivers are dry or seasonal, with the Kunene one of the few reliable hydro sites; importing from neighbouring grids has cost less than building large new stations; and the abundant sunshine now makes solar generation the fastest-growing domestic source.
